The Houthis ⁠- the Iran-backed group in Yemen, said on Thursday they had carried ⁠out ⁠a military ​operation targeting two Saudi ⁠oil tankers, identified as ENCELA and ⁠LAYLIA, saying the ​vessels violated ‌the ‌naval blockade imposed ‌by the group on Monday.
The Houthis’ announcement prompted the Saudi-led coalition to declare that it ⁠would respond “firmly”, in ​a ​move that threatens ​to disrupt ​global ‌energy supplies ​beyond ​the Gulf.
The Saudi authorities have not immediately confirmed the strike.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said it had received reports that a tanker had been struck by an unknown projectile and caught fire in the Red Sea, 70 nautical miles from Saudi Arabia’s Al Shuqaiq. At the time of writing there are no reported casualties and the projectile’s origin has not been specified.
Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran would respond in kind to any attack on its infrastructure, after Donald Trump’s threat to bomb a bridge or power plant for every ship targeted in the strait of Hormuz. “Our defence doctrine is clear: eye for an eye. Any aggression against Iran, including our infrastructure, will compel a powerful and decisive response,” Araghchi said on X.
Iran’s state broadcaster also quoted the Iranian military as saying that US threats “will have no result other than the expansion of the war”. It added that if the US acts on the threats, Iran will stop all Gulf oil flow and target oil, gas, electricity and economic infrastructure in the region.
Iran’s top negotiator and powerful parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, also warned on Wednesday that if Tehran cannot export its oil, no other country in the region would be able to do so. He wrote on X: “The equation of this war is clear: either all or none! In a region where we do not sell oil, no one will sell oil. If our security is not ensured, no infrastructure will be safe, and the security of the strait is in the absence of American forces. We have repeatedly said that the situation of the strait will not return to pre-war conditions. He also repeated that the strait of Hormuz “will not return to pre-war conditions”, as he has warned several times before.
It all came after Donald Trump threatened retribution against Iran in a post on Truth Social on Wednesday. “From this point forward, any time the Islamic Republic of Iran shoots at a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, whether it be by Missile, Rocket, Drone, or any other device or weapon, the United States will bomb and destroy ONE BRIDGE OR POWER PLANT, including those located next to, or in, the Capital City of Tehran,” the US president said on Truth Social. The threat came after the US conducted its 11th consecutive day of strikes on Iran, including on aircraft hangars and drone storage sites, as the renewed conflict continues to undermine diplomatic efforts to salvage an interim ceasefire deal.
Trump also attended the dignified transfer of four US service members killed in the Middle East over the weekend, the third such ceremony the US president has attended since he launched the war in Iran in February. Speaking to reporters on his way to Dover, Delaware, Trump called it “one of the hardest things to do as a president”. His message to grieving families, he said, will simply be “we love you, we love your child”.
The Trump administration signed a nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that could enable the kingdom to enrich its own uranium for nuclear reactors, US energy secretary Chris Wright said. As my colleague Patrick Wintour reported earlier, the timing of the announcement is controversial as the US’s war with Iran is being fought in part to prevent Tehran enriching uranium domestically and make it near-impossible for Iran to build a nuclear weapon. The plan is expected to be submitted to Congress for review, where it could face opposition among US lawmakers who fear a lack of monitoring safeguards to restrict Saudi Arabia’s uranium enrichment.
The Trump administration signed a nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that could enable the kingdom to enrich its own uranium for nuclear reactors, US Energy secretary Chris Wright said in a press release.
According to a statement from the Department of Energy, Wright and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, signed “a peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement” and “an accompanying bilateral safeguards agreement.”
The question of what those safeguards look like, given the potential for enriched uranium to be used to make nuclear weapons, will be closely scrutinized when the agreement is sent to Congress for review.
The two agreements, the press release said, “lay the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar partnership that advances several priority economic and strategic objectives, including nuclear nonproliferation.”
“These agreements reflect our two nations’ shared commitment to strengthening U.S.-Saudi commercial relations, delivering prosperity at home and security to our allies abroad,” Wright said in a statement. “Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world’s best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States.”
As our colleague Patrick Wintour reported earlier:
The timing of the announcement is controversial as the US’s war with Iran is being fought in part to prevent Tehran enriching uranium domestically and make it near-impossible for Iran to build a nuclear weapon.
The US-Saudi deal is expected to last 30 years and involve US firms such as Westinghouse in developing the programme.
It could allow for the building of a uranium enrichment facility in Saudi Arabia after a joint US-Saudi study. The proposal has been in discussion for years. At one point the Biden administration wanted to condition Saudi Arabia’s access to the technology on normalising relations with Israel, something Saudi Arabia is still refusing to do.
The plan is expected to be submitted to Congress for review, where it could face opposition among lawmakers who fear a lack of monitoring safeguards to restrict Saudi Arabia’s uranium enrichment.
Fatemeh Aman, an Iran expert and a former non-resident fellow at the Middle East Institute and a former senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, told the Guardian:
Iran is trying to balance deterrence with restraint. It wants to demonstrate that US military action carries costs while avoiding a full-scale war that could threaten the survival of the regime. Tehran therefore favours calibrated retaliation, enough to preserve credibility, but not enough to trigger overwhelming US escalation. A drawn-out war would be costly for both sides, but probably more so for Iran. The United States has greater military and economic resources, while Iran faces growing pressure on its economy, infrastructure, and domestic stability. That is why Tehran’s objective is to raise the costs for Washington, not to sustain an open-ended conflict.
Iran is already using missiles and drones against US bases and targets in Gulf states, while also attacking shipping and disrupting traffic through the strait of Hormuz. The most likely option is therefore a continuation of these attacks possibly with changes in intensity and target selection. Iran can also expand cyberoperations, covert attacks, and pressure through allied armed groups.
The more escalatory options would be larger attacks on Persian Gulf energy infrastructure or attempts to cause more sustained disruption to regional shipping. However, these would risk provoking an even broader US response and further alienating Gulf governments.
Iran still has the ability to impose significant regional and economic costs, but its capacity to sustain a prolonged war of attrition is more limited than that of the United States. Such a conflict would be damaging to both sides, but probably more damaging to Iran because of the imbalance in military resources and Iran’s greater economic and infrastructural vulnerability.
According to Aman, in the short term, the attacks are likely to strengthen the security establishment. Hardliners can argue that negotiations alone cannot guarantee Iran’s security and that military deterrence remains essential.
Over time, however, the conflict could expose deep divisions within the leadership over the costs of continued confrontation. If economic conditions worsen and military losses mount, debates over strategy are likely to become more pronounced, even if they remain largely behind closed doors.
The strikes are likely to delay parts of Iran’s nuclear program by damaging facilities, equipment, and infrastructure. However, they are unlikely to eliminate the program altogether. Iran retains technical expertise, scientific knowledge, and the ability to rebuild over time. Military action can slow the program, but it cannot permanently remove the underlying capability or motivation. Without a political agreement and an effective inspection regime, the strikes are more likely to buy time than provide a lasting solution.
Iran’s foreign ministry has said it is “shameful” that US lawmakers didn’t discuss the human suffering caused by the US-Israeli war on his country during a congressional hearing on additional funding for the conflict on Wednesday.
Esmaeil Baqaei wrote on X:
It is shameful that during the U.S. Congress hearing regarding the performance of the U.S. Secretary of War in the war against the Iranian nation, not even a single question was raised about the human dimensions of this brutal war, despite the fact that all of them are well aware that the U.S. military aggression against Iran has been an illegal war accompanied by countless war crimes, including the crimes of #Minab and #Lamard.
As you will remember, at least 175 people – most of them children – were killed on the first day of the war when a Tomahawk missile hit a girls’ elementary school in the southern Iranian city of Minab.
A preliminary US military investigation found that American forces were responsible. But while reports suggest that a secretive probe into the attack has concluded, some critics fear the Pentagon will bury the results under classifications to keep the worst mistakes secret from the public.
That same day, a strike hit a sports hall in Lamerd, also in southern Iran, killing at least 24 people, including teenage girls playing volleyball. The US was reportedly responsible for that too.
In a post on X, Iran’s deputy foreign minister said he met with 25 European ambassadors and chargé d’affaires in Tehran and outlined his country’s position regarding the conflict.
“I reminded them that in the 40-day war, we imposed a severe defeat on the aggressors. In this new round of military aggression as well, we will resolutely defend our homeland and national interests,” Kazem Gharibabadi posted.
“These wars have created no strategic gains for America and only endanger regional and global peace and security. I also said that Europe is expected to safeguard the United Nations Charter and international law and to condemn aggression,” he added.
“Of course, a few Europeans, such as Spain, adopted principled positions. European governments must take note that placing bases and territory at the disposal of the aggressor will rank them among the aggressors. Europe is expected to be the driving force of diplomacy, not a follower of the aggressor’s power.”
The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, rose 3.4% to $94.07 (£70) after briefly topping $95 to touch its highest price in nearly six weeks, AP reports.
That is up from less than $72 early this month, which is roughly where it was before the war with Iran. Rising oil prices are threaten to reaccelerate inflation. AP says that in turn could push the Federal Reserve and other central banks to raise interest rates, which would slow economies and undercut prices for stocks and other investments.

President Donald Trump is attending the dignified transfer today of four US service members killed in the Middle East. Trump will be at Dover Air Force Base in Delaware when the remains of the troops killed in action are returned to their families, the White House said.
Britain’s new prime minister has agreed to allow the US to continue to use UK airbases for bombing missions against Iran as the US steps up its attacks on the country. Andy Burnham endorsed a decision taken by his predecessor Keir Starmer at a Cobra meeting on Friday to allow the US to resume strikes from UK bases against Iranian missile launchers and sites around the strait of Hormuz.
A US missile struck the Iranian island of Larak on Wednesday, the Tasnim news agency reported, in the latest attack to target the Islamic republic’s islands in and around the strait of Hormuz. The islands have been hit multiple times as the two sides fight over the strategic waterway, which Iran has sealed following the collapse of a preliminary deal aimed at ending the war.
Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis have been recorded sending radio warnings to ships, the International Chamber of Shipping told AFP on Wednesday, after the rebels announced a naval blockade of Saudi Arabia. “We can confirm that the Houthis were recorded transmitting a warning message to ships in the region,” the ICS said.
The price of oil has breached the $95 a barrel mark for the first time in six weeks as the escalating Middle East conflict threatens further disruption to global supplies. The benchmark oil price rose sharply on Wednesday as renewed US-Iran aggression over the strait of Hormuz was compounded by Houthi threats to target vessels carrying Saudi oil through the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
The European Union ⁠Aviation Safety Agency on Wednesday added Jordan to the no-fly list, asking airlines not to operate withint the airspace as “the security situation has deteriorated rapidly”, Reuters reports. Iran has been targeting sites in Jordan and other US Gulf states amidst the renewed conflict. Last weekend, two US military personnel members were killed in an attack on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan.
Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani said that a new round of US-mediated talks between israel and Lebanon are set to take place in Italy on 4 August, AFP reports. This comes after a round of talks between the two countries in Rome last week.
The US military completed its 11th night of strikes on Iran, including on aircraft hangars and drone storage sites, as the renewed conflict continues to undermine diplomatic efforts to salvage an interim ceasefire deal.
The Jordanian army said it intercepted four Iranian missiles on Wednesday with two additional missile falling in an open area, AFP reports. The two missiles that the army did not intercept fell in “two remote, uninhabited areas, without causing any human casualties or material damage” the army said in a statement.
Iran has executed a man after finding him guilty of charges related to protests that swept the country last winter, according to AFP. The Iranian judiciary announced on Wednesday that Iran has executed a man identified as Mehdi Khanaki, who was arrested on 10 February in Karaj, west of Tehran, while in possession of a large arsenal. Khanaki “was condemned to death and the confiscation of all his property for having acted in favour of the Zionist and American regimes,” the website said. These allegations could not be independently confirmed.
In Lebanon, the focus is on “a complete Israeli withdrawal from the south”, Lebanese prime minister Nawaf Salam said on Wednesday. Salam was visiting Zawtar al-Gharbiya, one of several “pilot zones” intended to demonstrate that the Lebanese army can remove and disarm Hezbollah as part of a Washington-sponsored deal with Israel, AFP reports.
